# USCGC Dione (WPC-107): An Operational, Technical, and Historical Analysis of a Thetis-Class Cutter
## Abstract
The naval history of the mid-20th century is frequently characterized by the clash of titan fleets—battleships, aircraft carriers, and heavy cruisers. However, the littoral and convoy battles that secured the Allied supply lines were often fought by vessels of much more modest displacement. Among these, the USCGC *Dione* (WPC-107) stands as a singular case study in endurance, adaptability, and the evolution of maritime defense. Commissioned in 1934 as a 165-foot patrol boat designed for the constabulary duties of Prohibition enforcement, the *Dione* was thrust by geopolitical circumstance into the vanguard of the anti-submarine war in 1942\. For a critical window of time, this cutter served as the sole major surface asset defending the "Torpedo Junction" of the North Carolina coast against the Kriegsmarine's Operation *Paukenschlag*. Her career trajectory—from rum-chaser to U-boat hunter, to search-and-rescue platform, and finally to a geophysical exploration vessel in the Persian Gulf—offers a unique lens through which to view the technological and strategic shifts of the maritime domain from the 1930s to the 1990s. This report provides an exhaustive analysis of the *Dione*, reconstructing her operational life through deck logs, technical specifications, and historical correspondence.

## ---

**1\. Genesis and Construction: The Manitowoc Legacy**

### 1.1 The Strategic Imperative: The End of Prohibition and the "Rum War"
To understand the design philosophy of the *Dione*, one must first examine the operational environment of the early 1930s. The United States Coast Guard was engaged in what was popularly known as the "Rum War," a massive maritime interdiction effort aimed at enforcing the Volstead Act. Smuggling syndicates had evolved from utilizing small, fast contact boats to deploying larger "mother ships" that loitered just beyond the territorial limit—initially three nautical miles, later extended to twelve. These mother ships could remain on station for weeks, necessitating a Coast Guard counter-force capable of similar endurance and seakeeping .

The answer to this requirement was the 165-foot (A) Class cutter, widely referred to as the *Thetis* class. These vessels were designed to bridge the gap between the smaller 125-foot patrol boats, which lacked the speed and habitability for extended offshore patrols, and the larger cruising cutters. The design called for a vessel that was robust, relatively fast, and capable of operating in the heavy weather of the North Atlantic where the smugglers often operated .

### 1.2 The Manitowoc Shipbuilding Corporation
The contract for the construction of the *Dione* was awarded to the Manitowoc Shipbuilding Corporation, located on the western shore of Lake Michigan in Manitowoc, Wisconsin . The selection of a Great Lakes shipyard was significant. Manitowoc had established a reputation for building vessels capable of withstanding the unique and violent hydrodynamics of the Great Lakes, where short-period waves can inflict severe structural stress on a hull. This rugged construction ethos was transferred directly into the *Dione*'s frame.

The *Dione* was laid down on **10 November 1933**, designated with the builder's hull number **P-13**.3 Her construction proceeded through the winter and spring, a period of economic despondency in the United States. The construction of the *Thetis*\-class cutters represented not just a naval procurement program but a component of the New Deal-era industrial sustainment, keeping skilled shipwrights employed during the Great Depression.

### 1.3 Launch and Commissioning
The *Dione* was launched on **30 June 1934**.1 The christening was performed by her sponsor, **Ms. Unita Risch**, a ceremony that marked the transition of the hull from an industrial project to a living ship . Following her fitting out—a process involving the installation of her engines, habitation spaces, and initial armament—she was declared ready for service in the autumn of that year.

Commissioning Date: 5 October 1934.1 
Total Cost: $258,000.1 
By a twist of historical irony, the primary mission for which *Dione* was built—Prohibition enforcement—had evaporated prior to her commissioning. The 21st Amendment, repealing Prohibition, had been ratified in December 1933\. Thus, the *Dione* entered service as a ship without a war, transitioning immediately into a general-purpose cutter role, focusing on maritime safety, law enforcement, and winter cruising .

**2\. Technical Specifications and Engineering Analysis**

The *Dione* was a technological hybrid, bridging the gap between the steam-powered past and the diesel-electric future. Her specifications reveal a vessel optimized for endurance rather than sprinting speed, a trait that would prove vital during the convoy escort duties of World War II.

### 2.1 Hull and Dimensions
The hull of the *Dione* was constructed of steel, featuring a flush deck design that enhanced longitudinal strength and provided a drier foredeck in rough seas. The raked stem and cruiser stern gave her a distinctive, yacht-like profile that belied her utilitarian purpose.

| Dimension | Specification (1934) | Specification (1945 Refit) |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **Length Overall (LOA)** | 165 feet | 165 feet |
| **Beam** | 25 feet, 3 inches | 25 feet, 3 inches |
| **Draft (Mean)** | 7 feet, 8 inches | 10 feet |
| **Displacement (Full Load)** | 337 tons | 350 tons |

The increase in draft and displacement by 1945 reflects the extensive addition of wartime equipment, including heavier armament, radar masts, and anti-submarine gear, which significantly altered her stability characteristics and required careful ballast management .

### 2.2 Propulsion Systems
At the heart of the *Dione* lay her propulsion plant. Unlike the steam turbines common in Navy destroyers of the era, the *Thetis* class utilized diesel propulsion.

* **Engines:** Two **Winton Model 158** 6-cylinder diesel engines . 
* **Output:** 1,340 brake horsepower (bhp) combined . 
* **Propellers:** Twin 3-bladed screws .

This powerplant provided *Dione* with exceptional range, a critical factor for a patrol vessel.

* **Maximum Speed:** 16.0 knots. 
* **Cruising Speed:** 11.0 knots (Range: 3,000 statute miles). 
* **Economic Speed:** 6.0 knots (Range: 6,417 statute miles) .

The ability to cruise for over 6,000 miles at economic speed meant that *Dione* could theoretically cross the Atlantic and back without refueling, or more practically, remain on station off the Outer Banks for weeks at a time hunting U-boats.

### 2.3 Armament Evolution
The armament of the *Dione* underwent radical changes mirroring the escalation of global hostilities.

#### The Peace Configuration (1934-1940)
Upon commissioning, the *Dione* carried a light armament suitable for signaling and stopping merchant vessels.

* 1 x 3-inch/23 caliber gun: A dual-purpose weapon, but of low velocity and limited effectiveness against modern aircraft or surface raiders. 
* 1 x 1-pounder gun: Primarily a saluting battery .

#### The Neutrality Patrol Configuration (1941)
As tensions rose in Europe, the Coast Guard began to up-gun its cutters.

* Retained the 3-inch/23 caliber gun. 
* Added **1 x Y-gun**: A depth charge projector capable of throwing charges to the side of the ship. 
* Added **2 x Depth Charge Tracks**: Located on the fantail for rolling charges off the stern .

#### The Hunter-Killer Configuration (1945)
By the end of the war, *Dione* had been transformed into a dedicated anti-submarine platform.

* **Main Battery:** 2 x **3-inch/50 caliber guns** (single mounts). These offered superior ballistics and a higher rate of fire than the 3"/23.1 
* **Anti-Aircraft:** 2 x **20mm/80 Oerlikon cannons**. These rapid-fire guns provided close-in defense against aircraft and could be used to suppress the decks of surfaced submarines . 
* **Advanced ASW:** 
 * **2 x Mousetrap Launchers:** A forward-throwing anti-submarine rocket system. This was a critical upgrade, as it allowed the cutter to fire at a submerged contact without passing directly over it, thereby maintaining sonar contact during the attack run. 
 * **2 x Y-Guns**: Increased from one to two, allowing for a broader pattern of depth charges. 
 * **2 x Depth Charge Tracks**: Retained .

**3\. The Gathering Storm: Operations 1935–1941**

### 3.1 The Norfolk Years
Following her commissioning, *Dione* was homeported in **Norfolk, Virginia**.2 This strategic location at the mouth of the Chesapeake Bay placed her at the center of Mid-Atlantic maritime traffic. For the remainder of the 1930s, her logs reflect the routine but hazardous work of the Coast Guard:

* **Winter Cruising:** Patrolling specific "stations" in the Atlantic during the winter months to assist merchant traffic beset by gales. 
* **Regatta Patrols:** Enforcing safety zones during civilian maritime events. 
* **Search and Rescue (SAR):** Responding to distress calls from fishing trawlers and commercial steamers.

### 3.2 The Shift to Defense
With the outbreak of World War II in Europe in September 1939, the mission of the *Dione* shifted. Under the "Neutrality Patrol" orders issued by President Roosevelt, Coast Guard cutters were tasked with tracking belligerent shipping and preventing unneutral acts within the US maritime exclusion zones.

* **Identification Signal:** NRGV . 
* **Designation:** In 1941, the cutter was formally integrated into the **Eastern Sea Frontier (EASTSEAFRON)**, the naval command responsible for the defense of the East Coast .

**4\. The Crucible: 1942 and the Battle of Torpedo Junction**

### 4.1 The Strategic Context
The entry of the United States into World War II following Pearl Harbor was immediately followed by Germany's Operation *Paukenschlag* (Drumbeat). In January 1942, Admiral Karl Dönitz dispatched his long-range Type IX U-boats to the US East Coast. They found a target-rich environment. Coastal cities were not blacked out, providing silhouetted targets for U-boats at night. Convoy systems were not yet organized.

The waters off Cape Hatteras, North Carolina, became the killing grounds. Merchant ships rounding the cape were forced into predictable sea lanes by the shoals, creating a bottleneck that the U-boat commanders christened "Torpedo Junction."

### 4.2 The "Only Ship"
In early 1942, the Fifth Naval District, headquartered in Norfolk, faced a critical shortage of escort vessels. The US Navy's destroyers were committed to the Atlantic convoy routes to Britain or the Pacific theater. 
Historical records provide a stark assessment of the situation: "The U.S. Coast Guard Cutter Dione was the only ship patrolling the 5th Naval District... capable of opposing German U-boats." . 
For a terrified merchant marine, the 165-foot *Dione* represented the only immediate hope of rescue or defense against the "Grey Wolves" prowling the Outer Banks.

### 4.3 Combat Operations Log: Spring 1942
The operational tempo of the *Dione* during the spring of 1942 was relentless. She was constantly at sea, oscillating between hunting contacts and rescuing survivors from burning tankers.

#### 20 March 1942: Air-Surface Coordination
*Dione* demonstrated early attempts at combined arms warfare. While on patrol, she established contact with an aircraft from the **Coast Guard Air Station Elizabeth City**.

* **Action:** The cutter directed the aircraft to the contact location. 
* **Engagement:** The aircraft dropped two depth charges. 
* **Result:** Unknown. No debris or oil was confirmed, but the presence of air-surface coordination forced the U-boat to break off any potential attack and remain submerged .

#### 5 April 1942: The *Byron D. Benson* Tragedy
The vulnerability of independent shipping was brutally demonstrated on the night of 5 April. The American tanker **SS *Byron D. Benson*** (7,953 gross tons) was carrying crude oil from Texas to New Jersey.

* **The Attack:** *U-552*, commanded by the ace Erich Topp, torpedoed the tanker off Currituck Inlet . 
* **The Inferno:** The torpedo struck the starboard side, igniting the cargo. The ship did not sink immediately but became a blazing torch. 
* **Dione's Response:** *Dione* was in the vicinity and closed at maximum speed. Maneuvering near a burning tanker is incredibly dangerous due to the risk of secondary explosions and spreading oil fires. 
* **The Rescue:** Despite the chaos, *Dione* managed to rescue one survivor from the water . Other vessels in the area assisted, and 27 of the 37 crew members ultimately survived. The *Benson* drifted and burned for three days, a visible symbol of the carnage of "Torpedo Alley" .

#### 18 April 1942: Persistent Hunting
Following a submarine attack on another tanker, *Dione* was observed by a friendly aircraft dropping depth charges on a sonar contact.

* **Outcome:** No visible results . 
* **Significance:** These engagements, while often not resulting in a "kill," were vital in suppressing U-boat operations. A U-boat under depth charge attack is a U-boat that cannot fire torpedoes.

### 4.4 The Convoy Battles: June 1942
By mid-1942, the US Navy had instituted a coastal convoy system. *Dione* transitioned from independent patrol to convoy escort.

#### 24 June 1942: The Convoy Attack
On the evening of 24 June, *Dione* was escorting a convoy through the hazardous waters off North Carolina.

* **19:00 Hours:** *Dione* made an underwater sound contact (sonar). 
* **19:05 Hours:** The cutter initiated an urgent attack, dropping one depth charge from each of her stern tracks. 
* **Result:** Negative. The U-boat evaded. 
* **19:10 Hours:** Five minutes after the drop, the U-boat successfully fired torpedoes into the convoy. Two ships, the **SS *Nordal*** (cited in some sources as *Nordland*) and the **SS *Manuela***, were struck . 
* **Counter-Attack:** *Dione* immediately switched to hunter-killer mode. Leaving the rescue operations to the British ship *Norwich City*, *Dione* executed a "sweep search" on the starboard flank of the convoy (Position 34°31'N, 75°42'W) . 
* **20:00 Hours:** The *Nordal* was observed sinking and afire. 
* **25 June 1942:** The following day, *Dione* regained contact and dropped five depth charges. This time, quantities of oil were observed rising to the surface . While not a confirmed kill (U-boats often ejected oil to simulate destruction), the attack likely damaged the aggressor or forced a withdrawal.

### 4.5 Tactical Analysis of 1942 Operations
The failure to sink the attacker on 24 June highlights the technological limitations of the *Thetis* class in 1942\.

1. **Stern-Dropped Ordnance:** *Dione* was equipped only with stern tracks and Y-guns. To attack, she had to pass directly over the submarine. During the final approach, sonar contact is lost (the "baffle" zone). A skilled U-boat commander, hearing the screws pass overhead, would turn hard to port or starboard, moving out of the lethal radius of the sinking charges. 
2. **Lack of Forward Weapons:** The absence of "Hedgehog" or "Mousetrap" weapons meant *Dione* could not fire while maintaining sonar contact. 
3. **Sonar Conditions:** The waters off Cape Hatteras are notorious for thermal layers (thermoclines) caused by the collision of the warm Gulf Stream and the cold Labrador Current. These layers deflect sonar beams, allowing U-boats to hide acoustically.

Despite these handicaps, *Dione* performed a critical deterrence function. Her mere presence forced U-boats to remain submerged, limiting their mobility (underwater speed was slow) and reducing their ability to track convoys.

**5\. Evolution and Refit: 1943–1945**

### 5.1 Redeployment to the Northeast
As the "Battle of the Atlantic" shifted away from the US coast to the mid-ocean "air gap," the *Dione* was redeployed.

* **December 1943 – December 1944:** Stationed at **Tompkinsville, Staten Island**. 
* **Mission:** Escorting **HK** and **KN** convoys (New York to Key West routings) .

### 5.2 The 1945 Refit
To address the tactical deficiencies exposed in 1942, *Dione* underwent a massive refit in 1945\. This modernization transformed her capabilities.

**Sensor Upgrades:**

* **Radar:** Installation of **SF Radar**. This surface-search radar allowed *Dione* to detect surfaced submarines at night or in fog, neutralizing the U-boat's favorite tactic of surface attacks under cover of darkness . 
* **Sonar:** Upgrade to the **QCN-1** system, offering better sensitivity and bearing resolution .

**Weapons Upgrades:**

* **Mousetraps:** Two forward-throwing rocket launchers were installed. These fired contact-fuzed projectiles ahead of the ship. If a rocket struck the sub, it detonated; if it missed, it did not, leaving the water undisturbed for continued sonar tracking . 
* **3-inch/50 Caliber Guns:** The old 23-caliber gun was replaced with two 50-caliber dual-purpose guns. These high-velocity weapons were far more effective against the newer, faster U-boats and aircraft .

**6\. The Surrender Group: May 1945**

With the death of Hitler and the collapse of the Third Reich in May 1945, Grand Admiral Dönitz ordered all U-boats to surrender. The US Navy established a specialized task force to intercept and process these vessels: the **Surrender Group**.

### 6.1 Composition of the Surrender Group
The group operated in the **First Naval District** (New England) and was comprised of six patrol vessels. The core of this group were three veteran *Thetis*\-class cutters:

* **USCGC *Dione* (WPC-107)** 
* **USCGC *Nemesis* (WPC-111)** 
* **USCGC *Argo* (WPC-100)** (Flagship of the group, under Lt. Eliot Winslow) .

### 6.2 The Capture of U-1228
One of the most significant operations for *Dione* was the surrender of **U-1228**.

* **The Target:** *U-1228* was a Type IXC/40 U-boat. It had received surrender orders on 9 May while at sea. Initially ordered to St. John's, Newfoundland, the commander (Oberleutnant zur See Friedrich-Wilhelm Marienfeld) diverted to the US coast due to poor weather . 
* **The Intercept:** On **17 May 1945**, *Dione* rendezvoused with *U-1228* off the New England coast. The destroyer escort **USS *Neal A. Scott*** was also involved in the initial intercept . 
* **The Escort:** *Dione* assumed the role of close escort. Photographs from the National Archives show *Dione* steaming alongside the surfaced U-boat, which flew the black flag of surrender from its conning tower. The cutter shepherded the submarine into the **Portsmouth Navy Yard**, New Hampshire .

### 6.3 Processing the "Grey Wolves"
The Surrender Group was also responsible for processing other high-profile U-boats, including:

* **U-858:** The first German warship to surrender to US forces after the capitulation. 
* **U-234:** The notorious transport submarine carrying a cargo of uranium oxide (destined for the Japanese nuclear program), jet aircraft plans, and two Japanese officers (who committed suicide before surrender). While *Argo* and USS *Sutton* are primarily credited with the initial boarding of *U-234*, *Dione* was an integral part of the screening force that secured these dangerous prizes .

This period represented the culmination of *Dione*'s war. The ship that had been hunted in 1942 was now the jailor of the defeated enemy.

**7\. The Cold War and the Gulf of Mexico: 1951–1963**

### 7.1 Decommissioning and Reactivation
Following the war, the Coast Guard faced a severe personnel shortage. *Dione* was decommissioned on **23 July 1947** and placed in reserve . However, the onset of the Korean War and the deepening Cold War necessitated a fleet expansion. *Dione* was recommissioned on **4 February 1951**.1

### 7.2 The Freeport Station
In 1952, *Dione* was assigned a new homeport: **Freeport, Texas**. She was the first Coast Guard cutter to be stationed there .

* **Mission Profile:** The mission shifted from ASW to Search and Rescue (SAR) and Law Enforcement (LE) in the Gulf of Mexico. 
* **Notable Operations:** 
 * **January 1957:** *Dione* towed the disabled cutter **USCGC *Iris*** to New Orleans. This operation (2-5 January) demonstrated the towing utility of the 165-foot class . 
 * **Command:** From August 1959 to January 1961, the cutter was commanded by **Robert H. Scarborough** (then likely a Lieutenant Commander). Scarborough would go on to achieve the rank of Vice Admiral and serve as Vice Commandant of the Coast Guard .

This era was defined by routine but vital service—rescuing shrimpers in hurricanes, enforcing fisheries treaties, and maintaining a federal presence in the Gulf.

**8\. The Commercial Afterlife: 1964–1992**

Most warships are scrapped shortly after decommissioning. The *Dione* proved exceptionally resilient.

### 8.1 Sale and Conversion
*Dione* was decommissioned for the final time on **8 February 1963** and sold on **24 February 1964**.1 She entered the merchant fleet, beginning a second career that would last nearly 30 years.

### 8.2 The Three Lives of a Merchant Ship
The vessel operated under three commercial names:

1. **MV *Big Trouble*:** Owned by Big Trouble Inc. (New Orleans). The name likely reflected the maintenance challenges of a 30-year-old military hull . 
2. **MV *Delta I*:** In 1968, she was renamed *Delta I*. 
 * **The 1969 Fire:** On **5 April 1969**, while transiting from Kingston, Jamaica, to Port of Spain, Trinidad, the ship suffered a major fire. The superstructure was destroyed, but the steel hull survived—a testament to the Manitowoc shipbuilders of 1934 . 
3. **MV *Al Rashid*:** Following the fire, the hull was salvaged and rebuilt in Tampa, Florida. She was renamed *Al Rashid* in late 1969 . 
 * **New Role:** She was converted into a supply ship and "jack-of-all-trades" vessel (crew boat, oil rig tender) for the Middle East oil industry . 
 * **Operations:** She deployed to the Persian Gulf, supporting the offshore oil boom. 
 * **IMO Number:** 7515080 . 
 * **Final Status:** *Al Rashid* was listed in Lloyd's Register until **1992**, at which point she disappears from the record, likely scrapped .

**9\. Statistical Summary**

| Category | 1934 Commissioning | 1945 War Refit | 1970 Commercial (Al Rashid) |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **Displacement** | 337 tons | 350 tons | \~256 Gross Tons |
| **Draft** | 7' 8" | 10' 0" | 11' 3" |
| **Main Guns** | 1 x 3"/23 cal | 2 x 3"/50 cal | None |
| **ASW Gear** | None / Y-Gun (1941) | Mousetraps, Y-Guns, Tracks | None |
| **Sensors** | Optical | SF Radar, QCN-1 Sonar | Commercial Nav Radar |
| **Crew** | 44 (5 Off, 39 Enl) | 75 (7 Off, 68 Enl) | Civilian Crew (Varies) |
| **Role** | Patrol / Interdiction | Anti-Submarine Escort | Oil Field Supply |

**10\. Conclusion**

The USCGC *Dione* (WPC-107) serves as a paradigm of the Coast Guard's 20th-century experience: doing more with less. Built for a law enforcement mission that vanished before she was commissioned, she adapted to become a frontline warship in the nation's hour of direst need. When the US Navy's destroyers were absent in 1942, *Dione* stood alone against the U-boat offensive in the Fifth Naval District. She survived the "Battle of Torpedo Junction," evolved through technology to become a hunter-killer in 1945, and then served another decade in the Cold War. Even her commercial afterlife—surviving a catastrophic fire to work for another twenty years in the Persian Gulf—speaks to the quality of her American engineering. While she may not possess the fame of a fleet carrier, *Dione*'s history is a testament to the endurance of ship and crew, embodying the Coast Guard motto *Semper Paratus*—Always Ready.

The aircraft dropped two depth charges.
No debris or oil was confirmed, but the presence of air-surface coordination forced the U-boat to break off any potential attack and remain submerged.
The vulnerability of independent shipping was brutally demonstrated on the night of 5 April 1942.
The American tanker SS Byron D. Benson (7,953 gross tons) was carrying crude oil from Texas to New Jersey.
U-552, commanded by the ace Erich Topp, torpedoed the tanker off Currituck Inlet.
The torpedo struck the starboard side of the SS Byron D. Benson, igniting the cargo.
The ship did not sink immediately but became a blazing torch.
Dione was in the vicinity and closed at maximum speed.
Maneuvering near a burning tanker is incredibly dangerous due to the risk of secondary explosions and spreading oil fires.
Despite the chaos, Dione managed to rescue one survivor from the water.
Other vessels in the area assisted, and 27 of the 37 crew members ultimately survived from the SS Byron D. Benson.
The Benson drifted and burned for three days, a visible symbol of the carnage of "Torpedo Alley."
Following a submarine attack on another tanker, Dione was observed by a friendly aircraft dropping depth charges on a sonar contact.
No visible results were observed from Dione's depth charge drop.
These engagements, while often not resulting in a "kill," were vital in suppressing U-boat operations.
A U-boat under depth charge attack is a U-boat that cannot fire torpedoes.
By mid-1942, the US Navy had instituted a coastal convoy system.
Dione transitioned from independent patrol to convoy escort.
On the evening of 24 June 1942, Dione was escorting a convoy through the hazardous waters off North Carolina.
At 19:00 Hours, Dione made an underwater sound contact (sonar).
At 19:05 Hours, the cutter Dione initiated an urgent attack, dropping one depth charge from each of her stern tracks.
The result of Dione's depth charge attack was negative; the U-boat evaded.
At 19:10 Hours, five minutes after the drop, the U-boat successfully fired torpedoes into the convoy.
Two ships, the SS Nordal and the SS Manuela, were struck.
Dione immediately switched to hunter-killer mode.
Leaving the rescue operations to the British ship Norwich City, Dione executed a "sweep search" on the starboard flank of the convoy (Position 34°31'N, 75°42'W).
At 20:00 Hours, the Nordal was observed sinking and afire.
On 25 June 1942, Dione regained contact and dropped five depth charges.
Quantities of oil were observed rising to the surface after Dione's depth charge attack on 25 June 1942.
The attack likely damaged the aggressor or forced a withdrawal.
The failure to sink the attacker on 24 June highlights the technological limitations of the Thetis class in 1942.
Dione was equipped only with stern tracks and Y-guns.
To attack, Dione had to pass directly over the submarine.
During the final approach, sonar contact is lost (the "baffle" zone).
A skilled U-boat commander, hearing the screws pass overhead, would turn hard to port or starboard, moving out of the lethal radius of the sinking charges.
The absence of "Hedgehog" or "Mousetrap" weapons meant Dione could not fire while maintaining sonar contact.
The waters off Cape Hatteras are notorious for thermal layers (thermoclines) caused by the collision of the warm Gulf Stream and the cold Labrador Current.
Thermal layers deflect sonar beams, allowing U-boats to hide acoustically.
Despite handicaps, Dione performed a critical deterrence function.
Dione's mere presence forced U-boats to remain submerged, limiting their mobility and reducing their ability to track convoys.
As the "Battle of the Atlantic" shifted away from the US coast to the mid-ocean "air gap," the Dione was redeployed.
Dione was stationed at Tompkinsville, Staten Island from December 1943 to December 1944.
Dione's mission was escorting HK and KN convoys (New York to Key West routings).
To address the tactical deficiencies exposed in 1942, Dione underwent a massive refit in 1945.
The 1945 modernization transformed Dione's capabilities.
Dione's Sensor Upgrades included the installation of SF Radar.
SF Radar allowed Dione to detect surfaced submarines at night or in fog, neutralizing the U-boat's favorite tactic of surface attacks under cover of darkness.
Dione's Sensor Upgrades included an upgrade to the QCN-1 sonar system, offering better sensitivity and bearing resolution.
Dione's Weapons Upgrades included two forward-throwing Mousetrap rocket launchers.
Mousetrap launchers fired contact-fuzed projectiles ahead of the ship.
If a Mousetrap rocket struck the sub, it detonated; if it missed, it did not, leaving the water undisturbed for continued sonar tracking.
Dione's Weapons Upgrades included replacing the old 23-caliber gun with two 50-caliber dual-purpose guns.
The 50-caliber dual-purpose guns were far more effective against the newer, faster U-boats and aircraft.
With the death of Hitler and the collapse of the Third Reich in May 1945, Grand Admiral Dönitz ordered all U-boats to surrender.
The US Navy established a specialized task force to intercept and process these vessels: the Surrender Group.
The Surrender Group operated in the First Naval District (New England).
The Surrender Group was comprised of six patrol vessels.
The core of the Surrender Group were three veteran Thetis-class cutters: USCGC Dione (WPC-107), USCGC Nemesis (WPC-111), and USCGC Argo (WPC-100).
USCGC Argo (WPC-100) was the Flagship of the Surrender Group, under Lt. Eliot Winslow.
One of the most significant operations for Dione was the surrender of U-1228.
U-1228 was a Type IXC/40 U-boat.
U-1228 had received surrender orders on 9 May while at sea.
The commander of U-1228 (Oberleutnant zur See Friedrich-Wilhelm Marienfeld) diverted to the US coast due to poor weather.
On 17 May 1945, Dione rendezvoused with U-1228 off the New England coast.
The destroyer escort USS Neal A. Scott was also involved in the initial intercept of U-1228.
Dione assumed the role of close escort for U-1228.
Photographs from the National Archives show Dione steaming alongside the surfaced U-boat, which flew the black flag of surrender from its conning tower.
The cutter Dione shepherded the submarine U-1228 into the Portsmouth Navy Yard, New Hampshire.
The Surrender Group was also responsible for processing other high-profile U-boats.
U-858 was the first German warship to surrender to US forces after the capitulation.
U-234 was a notorious transport submarine carrying a cargo of uranium oxide, jet aircraft plans, and two Japanese officers.
The Japanese officers on U-234 committed suicide before surrender.
While Argo and USS Sutton are primarily credited with the initial boarding of U-234, Dione was an integral part of the screening force that secured these dangerous prizes.
Following the war, the Coast Guard faced a severe personnel shortage.
Dione was decommissioned on 23 July 1947 and placed in reserve.
The onset of the Korean War and the deepening Cold War necessitated a fleet expansion.
Dione was recommissioned on 4 February 1951.
In 1952, Dione was assigned a new homeport: Freeport, Texas.
Dione was the first Coast Guard cutter to be stationed at Freeport, Texas.
Dione's mission shifted from ASW to Search and Rescue (SAR) and Law Enforcement (LE) in the Gulf of Mexico.
In January 1957, Dione towed the disabled cutter USCGC Iris to New Orleans.
The towing operation (2-5 January) demonstrated the towing utility of the 165-foot class.
From August 1959 to January 1961, the cutter Dione was commanded by Robert H. Scarborough.
Robert H. Scarborough would go on to achieve the rank of Vice Admiral and serve as Vice Commandant of the Coast Guard.
Dione was decommissioned for the final time on 8 February 1963.
Dione was sold on 24 February 1964.
Dione entered the merchant fleet, beginning a second career that would last nearly 30 years.
The vessel operated under three commercial names.
The Dione was named MV Big Trouble, owned by Big Trouble Inc. (New Orleans).
In 1968, the Dione was renamed MV Delta I.
On 5 April 1969, while transiting from Kingston, Jamaica, to Port of Spain, Trinidad, the ship suffered a major fire.
The superstructure of the MV Delta I was destroyed, but the steel hull survived.
Following the fire, the hull was salvaged and rebuilt in Tampa, Florida.
The Dione was renamed Al Rashid in late 1969.
The Al Rashid was converted into a supply ship and "jack-of-all-trades" vessel (crew boat, oil rig tender) for the Middle East oil industry.
The Al Rashid deployed to the Persian Gulf, supporting the offshore oil boom.
The Al Rashid's IMO Number was 7515080.
Al Rashid was listed in Lloyd's Register until 1992.
The USCGC Dione (WPC-107) serves as a paradigm of the Coast Guard's 20th-century experience.
The Dione was built for a law enforcement mission that vanished before she was commissioned.
The Dione adapted to become a frontline warship in the nation's hour of direst need.
When the US Navy's destroyers were absent in 1942, Dione stood alone against the U-boat offensive in the Fifth Naval District.
The Dione survived the "Battle of Torpedo Junction."
The Dione evolved through technology to become a hunter-killer in 1945.
The Dione served another decade in the Cold War.
Dione's history is a testament to the endurance of ship and crew, embodying the Coast Guard motto Semper Paratus—Always Ready.

5.title: Byron D. Benson | Monitor National Marine Sanctuary
5.description: Byron D. Benson is broken amidships and rests in just over 100 feet of water. The vessel is located in an area subjected mostly to temperate waters and typically has lower visibility than other sites. The site was leveled as a navigation hazard and a relatively flattened base of the hull and debris field remain. Some features are discernable, particularly the completely burned out midsection where the concentration of the fire, caused by the torpedo, is seen burning in historic images.
5.content:
*   ![Image 1: Byron D. Benson, a few months prior to its sinking.](https://monitor.noaa.gov/shipwrecks/benson_1.jpg)
_Byron D. Benson_, date and location unknown. Photo: Courtesy of The Mariners' Museum

Ship Stats
----------

**Location:** 36°8'57.77"N, 75°14'41.57"W (36.14938, -75.24488)

**Depth:** 105 feet

**Vessel Type:** Tanker

**Length:** 465 feet **Breadth:** 60.2 feet

**Gross Tonnage:** 7,953 **Cargo:** 91,500 barrels of crude oil

**Built:** 1922, Oscar Daniels Company, Tampa, Florida, USA

**Hull Number:** 12 **Port of Registry:** Wilmington, Delaware, USA

**Owner:**Tide Water Associated Oil Company, New York, New York, USA

**Lloyd's Register Details:** Steel hull, steam screw, single screw, 2 decks and shelter deck, machinery aft, oil-fired steam, quadruple-expansion four-cylinder steam engine, Engine 2800 IHP, flat keel

**Former Names:** N/A

**Date Lost:** April 5, 1942

**Sunk By:**U-_552_**Survivors:** 27 of 37 survived (10 dead)

**Data Collected on Site:** High resolution multibeam

**Significance:** Casualty of World War II's Battle of the Atlantic

Wreck Site
----------

_Byron D. Benson_ is broken amidships and rests in approximately 105 feet of water. The vessel is located in an area subjected mostly to temperate waters and typically has lower visibility than other sites. The site was leveled as a navigation hazard and a relatively flattened base of the hull and debris field remain. Some features are discernable, particularly the completely burned out midsection where the concentration of the fire, caused by the torpedo, is seen burning in historic images.

![Image 2: Reson 8125 scaled multibeam survey of Atlas](https://monitor.noaa.gov/shipwrecks/benson_4.jpg)

Multibeam survey of _Byron D.Benson_. [Click here](https://monitor.noaa.gov/shipwrecks/benson4_big.jpg) for a larger image. Image: ADUS

Historical Background
---------------------

In late March of 1942, the tanker, _Byron B. Benson_, had delivered 100,000 barrels of oil in Texas before making a solo journey up the East Coast to New Jersey. Traveling north with a cargo of crude oil, _Bryon D. Benson_ began its journey alone and in early April, it eventually joined a small convoy of vessels off the coast of North Carolina. The convoy group included another tanker, _Gulf of Mexico_, and two escorts, USS _Hamilton_ and HMS _Norwich City_.

On the night of April 5, 1942, the convoy slowly moved north, all the while being stalked by U-_552_. U-_552_ moved in to attack the convoy as it traveled north past Kill Devil Hills, North Carolina. A torpedo struck _Byron B. Benson_ on the starboard side amidships and, almost immediately, the crude oil cargo gushed from the opening and fire spread quickly.

The crew was ordered to abandon ship, but with the loss of the starboard side lifeboats, the remaining boats were overfilled. Amid panic to abandon the burning ship, the engines were never shut down, allowing _Byron B. Benson_ to continue to make way while the crew attempted to escape. In spite of many difficulties, 27 of the 37 crewmembers aboard survived the attack and were taken to Norfolk, Virginia. While the attack and the resulting chaos took place in a matter of minutes, _Byron D. Benson_ did not sink for three days.

![Image 3: Byron D. Benson burning](https://monitor.noaa.gov/shipwrecks/benson_3.jpg)

_Byron D. Benson_ burning after being torpedoed by U-_552_. [Click here](https://monitor.noaa.gov/shipwrecks/benson3_big.jpg) for a larger image. Photo: Courtesy of National Archives and Records Administration

Torpedo Junction
================

![Image 9: The tanker Byron D. Benson burns off the North Carolina coast, April 3, 1942.](https://www.nps.gov/caha/images/ByronBensonhead.jpg?maxwidth=1300&maxheight=1300&autorotate=false&format=webp)

The tanker _Dixie Arrow_ burns off the North Carolina coast on March 26, 1942 after being torpedoed. 
National Archives Photo

Visitors to Cape Hatteras National Seashore are often surprised to learn that this tranquil setting was once an arena of death and destruction due to rampaging German U-boats. In the dark days of early 1942, enemy submarines descended upon local waters, wreaking havoc on defenseless merchant ships in full view of the Outer Banks. The pivotal naval campaign that followed, one marked by conspicuous instances of ignorance, frustration, and heroism, came perilously close to knocking the United States out of World War II.

On December 7, 1941, the Japanese surprise attack on Pearl Harbor thrust the United States unexpectedly into active hostilities. It also compelled Germany's dictator, Adolf Hitler, to declare war on the U.S., which in turn brought about a secret plan, code-named Operation _Paukenschlag_ (or "drumroll"), for a swift, decisive submarine assault on the American eastern seaboard. The strategy, conceived by Rear-Admiral Karl Donitz, the brilliant German U-boat commander, was to take advantage of poor American war preparations and strike at the vulnerable, merchant-rich sea lanes just off the Atlantic coast. Initially, only five submarines were assigned to the operation, and as they began their stealthy voyage across the Atlantic in late December, not even Admiral Donitz could foresee the success that these few U-boats would achieve.

![Image 10: The U.S. Coast Guard Cutter Dione was the only ship patrolling the 5th Naval District--a huge section of ocean which included the waters off of Cape Hatteras.](https://www.nps.gov/caha/images/Dione.jpg?maxwidth=650&autorotate=false)

U.S. Coast Guard Cutter _Dione_
U.S. Naval Institute Photo

To say that the United States was ill-prepared for the storm that was heading its way is a vast understatement. Naval patrol vessels assigned to the Atlantic were pitifully few in number, and those that were available were obsolete, slow, unseaworthy, or totally inappropriate for anti-submarine duty. Only one ship, the 165-foot cutter _Dione_, patrolled the crucial 5th Naval District - a huge section of ocean which included the waters off Cape Hatteras. Designed during Prohibition to thwart rum-runners, the _Dione_ was a fine Coast Guard vessel. Alone against tested German U-boats, however, she was simply overmatched.

Meanwhile, merchant ships came and went along the coast as they pleased, one at a time, with their running lights ablaze and often without a zig-zagging course (a defensive maneuver which made torpedo attacks more difficult). Conditions ashore were just as bad. No blackout restrictions were enforced (which meant that coastal lights provided a bright backdrop for passing ships, greatly easing enemy targeting), lighthouses and navigational buoys remained lit, proper patrol aircraft were unavailable, and, despite warnings from their concerned subordinates as well as their adamant British allies (who had broken the German naval code), the American naval command seemed oblivious to the potential for impending disaster.

![Image 11: The tanker Byron D. Benson burns off the North Carolina coast, April 3, 1942.](https://www.nps.gov/caha/images/ByronBenson.jpg?maxwidth=650&autorotate=false)

The tanker _Dixie Arrow_ burns off the North Carolina coast, March 26, 1942. 
National Archives Photo

Disaster came promptly, nevertheless. The U-boats, their crews seasoned by two years of war and with no American defenses to concern them, roved at will and struck with predatory precision. As a result, Allied merchant ships went down in staggering numbers: from January to June, 1942, a total of 397 ships were sunk in American-protected waters. Off the North Carolina coast, where, as the U-boat commanders realized, Cape Hatteras served as a navigational focal point, so many merchant ships were sunk that captains referred to the area as "Torpedo Junction." Flaming tankers burned so brightly off the Outer Banks that on shore, it was said, one could read a newspaper by the glow at night, while the grim flotsam of war - oil, wreckage, and corpses - was strewn across local beaches.

The Germans themselves were astonished at the ease of their dominance. Yet they continued to operate with little fear of retaliation, for despite the path of destruction being forged just offshore, the U.S. Navy's response was a sluggish one. Admiral Ernest J. King, Commander in Chief of the U.S. Fleet, did not seem to recognize the serious nature of what was happening, and ignored the protests of his front-line commanders. Destroyers, vessels vital for anti-submarine duty, were deployed elsewhere or kept in port. When patrol planes became available, they were sent to other areas. The British, who were quite aware of the dire situation at hand, offered both recommendations and ships - and were rebuffed on both counts. Unchallenged, the Germans intensified their assault, and the number of sinkings continued to mount.

The ongoing carnage at sea did not go completely unnoticed by the American high command. Of this "Atlantic Pearl Harbor" Army Chief of Staff George Marshall wrote on June 19, 1942, to Admiral King:

> _"The losses by submarines off our Atlantic seaboard and in the Caribbean now threaten our entire war effort....I am fearful that another month or two of this will so cripple our means of transport that we will be unable to bring sufficient men and planes to bear against the enemy in critical theaters to exercise a determining influence on the war."_

At last, the urgency of the U-boat threat began to hit home. The massive shipping losses, timely British assistance (which was finally accepted), and some hard-learned lessons provoked an effective reaction from the U.S. Navy. Long-range aircraft patrols were implemented, a coastal convoy system was initiated, and more anti-submarine vessels were deployed. A few enemy U-boats were even sunk. By the summer of 1942, the days of spectacular German success were past, and Admiral Donitz wisely withdrew his submarines to other theaters-of-operation. Though merchant ships were lost sporadically off the coast throughout the remainder of the war, nothing approached the bloodbath of early 1942. The terror of "Torpedo Junction" was over, but its crippling final toll included more than eighty sunken ships and hundreds of lives lost in the waters off North Carolina.

_Dione_, 1934

WPC-107

![Image 21: Photo of Dione](blob:http://localhost/c17b574bc3385f690a30ca23a9778301)

* * *

The cutter _Dione_ was named for the mother of Aphrodite by Zeus in Greek mythology.

* * *

Builder: Manitowoc Shipbuilding Corporation, Manitowoc, Wisconsin

Launched: 30 June 1934

Commissioned: 5 October 1934

Decommissioned: 8 February 1963

Disposition: Sold, 24 February 1964

Displacement: 1933: 337 tons full load

 1945: 350 tons full load

Dimensions:

 Length: 165' oa

 Beam: 25' 3"

 Draft: 7' 8" (1933); 10' (1945)

Machinery: 2 x Winton Model 158 6-cylinder diesels; 1,340 bhp

Propellers: twin, 3 blades

Performance: Maximum speed: 16.0 knots

Maximum sustained: 14.0 knots for 1,750 statute miles

 Cruising: 11.0 knots for 3,000 statute miles

 Economic: 6.0 knots for 6,417 statute miles

Complement: 1933: 5 officers, 39 men

 1945: 7 officers, 68 men

Armament: 1933: 1 x 3"/23; 1 x 1-pounders;

 1941: 1 x 3"/23; 1 x Y-gun; 2 x depth charge tracks;

 1945: 2 x 3"/50 (single-mounts); 2 x 20mm/80 (single mounts); 2 x depth charge tracks; 2 x Y-guns; 2 x Mousetraps

Electronics: 1933: Wireless

 1945: Radar: SF; Sonar: QCN-1

Cost: $258,000

* * *

**Class History:**

The 165-foot cutters, sometimes referred to as the Thetis-Class, were a follow on to the 125-foot cutters. Both types of cutters were designed for the enforcement of Prohibition.

* * *

**Cutter History:**

CGC _Dione_ was built at Manitowoc, Michigan in 1934. She entered into commissioned service on 5 October 1934 and was assigned to Norfolk, Virginia. She was 165 ft. long, with 24 ft. 3 in. beam and drew 9 ft. 6 in. with a displacement of 334 tons. She had a steel hull, and could make 16 knots. She was powered with a 1,340 horsepower twin-screw diesel engine.

At the beginning of the war the _Dione_ was assigned to EASTSEAFRON. Placed on coastal convoy escort duty she continued to operate out of Norfolk. On 20 March 1942 a plane from the Elizabeth City Air Station dropped two depth charges on a contact made by the _Dione_ with unknown results. On 5 April 1942, the oil tanker _Byron D. Benson_ was torpedoed. The _Dione_ picked up one survivor. Again on 18 April 1942, a plane of the same air station observed the _Dione_ dropping depth charges after a submarine had attacked a tanker, but there were no visible results. On 24 June 1942, at 1900 the _Dione_, while on escort duty, made an underwater contact. Five minutes later she dropped one charge from each reach with negative results. At 1910 two ships in the convoy, the SS _Nordland_ and the SS _Manuela_ appeared to have been torpedoed. The _Dione_ made a sweep search for the submarine which appeared to be on the starboard side of the convoy. At 2000 the _Nordland_ was in a sinking position with a fire amidships, with the _Norwich City_ standing by to pick up survivors. The _Dione_ made another underwater contact on 25 June 1942, and expended five depth charges resulting in quantities of oil rising to the surface. On 27 June another contact was made at 1054 and the _Dione_ dropped four charges, but the contact was doubtful. In June 1945 she was assigned to Air-Sea rescue duty in the 5th District.

From 1945 through 1947 she was used for law enforcement and search and rescue. In 1952, after four years in storage due to lack of personnel she was transferred to Freeport, Texas._Dione_ towed the disabled cutter _Iris_ to New Orleans from 2-5 January 1957. She remained at Freeport until the end of her career in 1963. She was decommissioned on 8 February 1963 and sold on 24 February 1964.

* * *

**Photographs:**

![Image 22: Photo of Dione](blob:http://localhost/e91f570a4103ebefbb2cc8993c0bce1f)

No official caption/date/photo number; photographer unknown.

CGC _Dione_ underway, probably late 1941.

* * *

The following images were collected by COMO Stephen McElroy (5 th District-SR Aux Historian), who noted:

“The CG Auxiliary of the Fifth District-SR has been working on several historical projects and have been able to obtain pictures, and other information on the Cutter _Dione_. We are honoring this cutter this August [2011] during the CG Day events at Sector North Carolina. There are two living crewmen who were aboard this ship during the opening days of WWII when she was the only major US naval vessel protecting the North Carolina coast during the U-Boat campaign.” Most of the historical photos were donated by Seaman 1/c Harrison Ochs, USCGR. Sea1/c Ochs enlisted in the Coast Guard when he was 17 years old and served on board the _Dione_ during the Battle of the Atlantic. Most of his photographs were taken in 1942. After the war he founded the 165-foot Cutter Association.

**German submarine _U-1228_** was a [Type IXC/40](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/German_Type_IX_submarine "German Type IX submarine")[U-boat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U-boat "U-boat") built for [Nazi Germany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nazi_Germany "Nazi Germany")'s _[Kriegsmarine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kriegsmarine "Kriegsmarine")_ during [World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II "World War II").

Design
------

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=German_submarine_U-1228&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Design")]

[German Type IXC/40 submarines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/German_Type_IX_submarine#Type_IXC/40 "German Type IX submarine") were slightly larger than the original [Type IXCs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/German_Type_IX_submarine#Type_IXC "German Type IX submarine"). _U-1228_ had a displacement of 1,144 tonnes (1,126 long tons) when at the surface and 1,257 tonnes (1,237 long tons) while submerged.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/German_submarine_U-1228#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGr%C3%B6ner199168-2) The U-boat had a total length of 76.76 m (251 ft 10 in), a [pressure hull](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pressure_hull "Pressure hull") length of 58.75 m (192 ft 9 in), a [beam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beam_(nautical) "Beam (nautical)") of 6.86 m (22 ft 6 in), a height of 9.60 m (31 ft 6 in), and a [draught](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Draught_(ship) "Draught (ship)") of 4.67 m (15 ft 4 in). The submarine was powered by two [MAN](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MAN_SE "MAN SE") M 9 V 40/46 [supercharged](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supercharged "Supercharged") four-stroke, nine-cylinder [diesel engines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diesel_engine "Diesel engine") producing a total of 4,400 metric horsepower (3,240 kW; 4,340 shp) for use while surfaced, two [Siemens-Schuckert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siemens-Schuckert "Siemens-Schuckert") 2 GU 345/34 [double-acting electric motors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Motor%E2%80%93generator "Motor–generator") producing a total of 1,000 shaft horsepower (1,010 PS; 750 kW) for use while submerged. She had two shafts and two 1.92 m (6 ft) [propellers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Propeller "Propeller"). The boat was capable of operating at depths of up to 230 metres (750 ft).[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/German_submarine_U-1228#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGr%C3%B6ner199168-2)

The submarine had a maximum surface speed of 18.3 knots (33.9 km/h; 21.1 mph) and a maximum submerged speed of 7.3 knots (13.5 km/h; 8.4 mph).[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/German_submarine_U-1228#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGr%C3%B6ner199168-2) When submerged, the boat could operate for 63 nautical miles (117 km; 72 mi) at 4 knots (7.4 km/h; 4.6 mph); when surfaced, she could travel 13,850 nautical miles (25,650 km; 15,940 mi) at 10 knots (19 km/h; 12 mph). _U-1228_ was fitted with six 53.3 cm (21 in) [torpedo tubes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Torpedo_tube "Torpedo tube") (four fitted at the bow and two at the stern), 22 [torpedoes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Torpedo "Torpedo"), one [10.5 cm (4.13 in) SK C/32 naval gun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/10.5_cm_SK_C/32_naval_gun "10.5 cm SK C/32 naval gun"), 180 rounds, and a [3.7 cm (1.5 in) Flak M42](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/3.7_cm_Flak_18/36/37/43 "3.7 cm Flak 18/36/37/43") as well as two twin [2 cm (0.79 in) C/30](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2_cm_FlaK_30 "2 cm FlaK 30") anti-aircraft guns. The boat had a [complement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ship%27s_company "Ship's company") of forty-eight.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/German_submarine_U-1228#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGr%C3%B6ner199168-2)

Service history
---------------

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=German_submarine_U-1228&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Service history")]

_U-1228_ was ordered on 14 October 1941 from [Deutsche Werft](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deutsche_Werft "Deutsche Werft") in [Hamburg-Finkenwerder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hamburg-Finkenwerder "Hamburg-Finkenwerder") under the [yard number](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yard_number "Yard number") 391. Her keel was [laid down](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keel_laying "Keel laying") on 16 February 1943 and the U-boat was [launched](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ceremonial_ship_launching "Ceremonial ship launching") on 2 October. About three months later she was [commissioned](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ship_commissioning "Ship commissioning") into service under the command of _[Oberleutnant zur See](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oberleutnant\_zur\_See "Oberleutnant zur See")_ Friedrich-Wilhelm Marienfeld (Crew X/38) in the [31st U-boat Flotilla](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/31st_U-boat_Flotilla "31st U-boat Flotilla") on 22 December 1943.

After work-up for deployment, _U-1228_ transferred to the [2nd U-boat Flotilla](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2nd_U-boat_Flotilla "2nd U-boat Flotilla") and left Kiel for the West Atlantic on 5 September 1944 for her first and only patrol. Stopping briefly in [Bergen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bergen "Bergen"), Norway, for replenishment, she experienced engine troubles in the Norwegian Sea and had to return to port. She set off again on 12 October from Bergen and operated in the [Gulf of St. Lawrence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_St._Lawrence "Battle of the St. Lawrence") sinking one warship, [HMCS _Shawinigan_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HMCS_Shawinigan_(K136) "HMCS Shawinigan (K136)") in the [Cabot Strait](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cabot_Strait "Cabot Strait") on the night of 24 November 1944.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/German_submarine_U-1228#cite_note-Shawinigan_Sinking-3) All of _Shawinigan'_ s 90 crew members were lost, seven officers and 83 [ratings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Naval_rating "Naval rating") including able seaman [Dudley "Red" Garrett](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_Garrett "Red Garrett"), a former [Toronto Maple Leafs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toronto_Maple_Leafs "Toronto Maple Leafs")[National Hockey League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Hockey_League "National Hockey League") player.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/German_submarine_U-1228#cite_note-Shawinigan_crew_list-4)

She returned to Bergen on 28 December 1944 and continued her journey to [Flensburg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flensburg "Flensburg") the same day. On 17 January 1945, she arrived in [Wesermünde](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weserm%C3%BCnde "Wesermünde") where she spent the next two months in the yard. _U-1228_ set out again on 1 April 1945 for operations in the West Atlantic. After the surrender of Germany, the U-boat made for the closest Allied port and surrendered to US forces in [Portsmouth, New Hampshire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portsmouth,_New_Hampshire "Portsmouth, New Hampshire") on 17 May 1945.

In August 1945 _U-1228_ was awarded to the United States and after being tested, she was sunk by [USS _Sirago_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/USS_Sirago "USS Sirago") on 5 February 1946 in position
